title: What is inflation? Why money loses value.
subtitle: Inflation isn't an accident. It is a built-in feature of every modern economy.
openingQuestion: Your parents remember a bowl of phở costing 500 đồng in 1990; today it is 70,000. Over 34 years, how much purchasing power did the đồng lose?
openingOptions: Impossible to say, because phở doesn't represent inflation
None, because money is still money
99.3% of its purchasing power: 1 đồng in 1990 is worth 0.007 today
About 50%, because economic growth offsets the rest
explanation: A bowl of phở at 500 đồng in 1990 costs roughly 70,000 today - a 140-fold rise over about three decades. What is worth noticing is not the number 140 but where it came from: an average inflation rate of only a few percent a year. Accumulate that for long enough and a rate that sounds harmless consumes the whole purchasing power of the currency. This is why holding cash over a long horizon is a risky decision, even though it feels like the safest option available.

diagram.label: Prices rise a few percent every year
The same money buys fewer goods
Compounded over decades, that becomes many times over
An investment must beat inflation to hold its real value

realWorldExample.description: Zimbabwe went through hyperinflation of 89.7 billion percent a month. A 100-trillion Zimbabwe dollar note was not enough to buy a loaf of bread.

quiz.question: What is the main mechanism that causes inflation?
options: Businesses raise prices together to widen their profit margins
Too much money chasing too few goods in the economy
Households save too little relative to what they earn
A rise in world oil prices, which is the only real cause
quiz.explanation: Inflation has two main sources: demand-pull (too much money in the economy) and cost-push (raw materials becoming more expensive). They usually occur at the same time.

quiz.question: Why is inflation of about 2% considered healthy?
options: Because the IMF requires member countries to hold this level
Because 2% is roughly what offsets depreciation on fixed assets
Because it encourages people to spend and invest today
Because businesses need 2% price rises to protect their margins
quiz.explanation: Moderate inflation creates pressure to spend: money will lose value, so putting it to work today is better than holding it. Deflation is more dangerous, because everyone postpones purchases waiting for prices to fall further.

quiz.question: Scenario: You hold 100 million VND in a savings account paying 6% a year. Average inflation runs at 4% a year. After 5 years, has your real purchasing power risen or fallen, and by how much?
options: Up 30% (= 6% × 5 years, ignoring inflation entirely)
Unchanged, because the interest rate offsets inflation
Down 20% (= 4% × 5 years, ignoring the interest)
Up about 10% (= (6% − 4%) × 5 years, the real rate)
quiz.explanation: Real rate = nominal rate − inflation = 6% − 4% = 2% a year. After 5 years, real purchasing power is up by roughly 10% (2% × 5). Where the rate is below inflation, you lose purchasing power even as the balance grows.

quiz.question: Scenario: A savings account pays 6% a year while inflation runs at 4% a year. What happens to your purchasing power after one year?
options: Up about 2%, the part of the interest that beats inflation
Up 6%, because bank interest is already a real return
Down 4%, because inflation erodes the whole deposit
Up 10% (= 6 + 4, adding instead of subtracting)
quiz.explanation: The balance rises 6% but prices rise 4% too, so what you can additionally buy is only about 2%. This is why a 5% return during 7% inflation is still making you poorer, even though the number on every statement is larger than the month before.

quiz.question: Why is deflation considered more dangerous than mild inflation?
options: Because deflation always arrives alongside a sharp rate rise
Because people postpone buying, demand falls, the economy shrinks
Because cheaper goods thin out profits, although firms can cope with it
Because deflation devalues money faster than inflation does
quiz.explanation: When prices are falling, waiting is always the better move, so spending gets postponed; weaker demand pushes businesses to cut prices again and cut jobs, and the loop feeds itself. Inflation of 2% keeps that spiral from starting.

keyTakeaways: Inflation erodes the purchasing power of money, accumulating year over year
Around 2% is the healthy target: it encourages spending and avoids deflation
An investment must return more than inflation to preserve real wealth

practicePrompt.question: If a savings rate is only 4% while inflation is 5%, what happens?
options: Real purchasing power rises
Real purchasing power is unchanged
Real purchasing power falls
Nothing changes, the rate is already enough
practicePrompt.explanation: The real rate is negative whenever the interest rate is below inflation. You hold more money in nominal terms but less purchasing power.

summary.keyIdea: Inflation measures purchasing power lost over time.
summary.commonMistake: Watching the number of đồng instead of what they can buy.
summary.action: Check whether your savings are actually gaining purchasing power or just gaining digits.

application.title: Apply it now
application.message: When you compare investment options, compare their real returns - after inflation has been subtracted.

sections.text: Your parents remember a bowl of phở costing 500 đồng in 1990; today it costs 70,000. That figure is not small talk - it is living proof of how quietly inflation does its damage.
What is inflation, and why is it always with us?

Inflation is the general level of prices for goods and services rising over time, so that one unit of currency buys fewer goods. It is not an economic 'accident' but an almost inherent feature of every modern economy, because the money supply usually grows faster than the real goods available in that economy.
140 times over in 34 years - what does that figure tell us?

70,000 divided by 500 is 140 - the price of phở has risen 140-fold. Put another way, 500 đồng in 1990 had the purchasing power of 70,000 đồng today; and 1 đồng held in your pocket across those 34 years has lost 99.3% of its original purchasing power, if it was held as cash earning nothing. This is exactly why 'cash is safe' becomes a risky decision over a long horizon.

items: Inflation erodes the purchasing power of money over time, accumulating year by year
A target of 2% a year is what many central banks regard as 'healthy' - enough to encourage spending, and enough to avoid the stagnation deflation brings
An investment has to return MORE than inflation before it genuinely preserves the value of your wealth

sections.label: What this means in practice
sections.text: If your savings earn 5% a year while inflation runs at 4% a year, you are only genuinely 1% a year better off - not the 5% the statement shows. This is the real interest rate, which later lessons cover in more depth.

lines: Understanding inflation reframes the goal: the objective is not to 'keep money' but to keep and grow purchasing power over time.
